target_audience: University students in Computer Science, Engineering, or Mathematics

sections.title: The Big Picture: What is Convolution?
sections.content: Introduce the concept of convolution as a way to 'blend' two sets of information. Explain that in the discrete world, it's about how one sequence (the signal) is modified by another (the filter/kernel). Use the analogy of a 'weighted moving average'.
sections.example: Imagine a chef mixing ingredients: the base flavor is the 'signal', and the spice intensity added over time is the 'kernel'. The resulting taste profile is the convolution.

sections.title: Prerequisite: Discrete Signals and Indices
sections.content: Briefly review discrete sequences represented as arrays. Define $x[n]$ as the input signal and $h[n]$ as the impulse response (filter). Explain the index 'n' as discrete time or spatial steps.
sections.example: A signal $x = [1, 2, 3]$ and a filter $h = [0.5, 1]$. Visualization: A series of vertical bars on a 2D graph.

sections.title: The Math: Flip, Slide, Multiply, Add
sections.content: Break down the formula $(x * h)[n] = \sum x[k]h[n-k]$. Use a step-by-step visual animation: 1. Flip the filter $h$. 2. Slide it across $x$. 3. Multiply overlapping elements. 4. Sum the results to get the output at index $n$.
sections.example: Calculating $([1, 2, 3] * [0.5, 1])$. Step 1: Flip $[0.5, 1]$ to $[1, 0.5]$. Step 2: Slide and multiply. Visual: The flipped filter sliding under the signal bars like a moving window.

sections.title: Expanding to 2D: The Image Matrix
sections.content: Transition from 1D sequences to 2D grids (images). Explain that pixels are just numbers in a matrix. A 2D convolution uses a small square matrix (kernel) that slides over the image from top-left to bottom-right.
sections.example: A 3x3 'Identity Kernel' (1 in the center, 0 elsewhere) passing over a 5x5 grid. Show the 'Focus Window' highlighting the current calculation area.

sections.title: Application: Pixel-Bot’s Vision Enhancement
sections.content: Introduce 'Pixel-Bot', a small robot trying to navigate a foggy environment. Demonstrate how convolution is used for edge detection (Sobel filter) and blurring (Gaussian filter) to help Pixel-Bot 'see' better.
sections.example: Pixel-Bot applies a 'Blur Kernel' to a noisy photo to smooth out graininess, then an 'Edge Kernel' to highlight the outlines of a doorway, turning raw pixels into meaningful shapes.

sections.title: Summary and Real-World Impact
sections.content: Recap the 'Flip-Slide-Sum' mechanism. Briefly mention that this is the fundamental operation behind Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs) used in modern AI like face recognition and autonomous driving.
sections.example: Visual recap: A montage of a 1D wave, a filtered photo, and a self-driving car’s camera feed, all powered by the same math.
